en: *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra*, Scroll One; also titled *The Diamond Cutter of Prajñā*.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
The Buddha-dharma produced herein is without equal, Manifesting the Dharma-realm as supreme and foremost;
A collection of vajra-like phrases and meanings, Into which no holy ones can enter.
This Minor Vajra Pāramitā reveals its power through such names;
having heard the teachings and their meanings as expounded by the wise, may you in turn explain them to us.
I take refuge in those of that kind and these of this sort, and I prostrate with a perfectly upright mind;
I shall diligently establish their meaning and explain the continuity for the sake of myself and others.
The Commentary states:
Once these seven categories of meaning have been established, this *prajñāpāramitā* is thereby established.

The seven categories of meaning are: first, the non-interruption of the lineage; second, the aspect of initiating practice; third, the locus where practice resides; fourth, the remedies; fifth, non-loss; sixth, the stages (*bhūmi*); and seventh, the establishment of names.
These seven meanings are established within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and are therefore termed "meaningful phrases" (*arthapada*).

Among them, the first six meaningful phrases demonstrate the culmination of the bodhisattva’s activities, while the seventh meaningful phrase demonstrates the establishment of this dharma-gate; thus should it be understood.
This Prajñāpāramitā circulates in the world so that the lineage of the Buddhas may not be interrupted.
To manifest this meaning— that the lineage of the Buddhas shall remain uninterrupted— the Elder Subhūti, at the beginning of the sutra,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas."

And so forth. Second, regarding the characteristics of the arousal [of the mind], it is as the sūtra says: "How does a bodhisattva, within the Mahāyāna, arouse the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? and so on.
Regarding the "abodes of the three types of conduct," this refers to the abodes of the modes of activity that are initiated.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are eighteen kinds:
first, the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
The Sūtra says: "All Bodhisattvas give rise to such a thought: 'All sentient beings whatsoever... and so forth.

The Sūtra says: "Without dwelling on things, one practices giving," and so forth.

Fifteenth, at the time of realizing the Path, one remains far removed from the agitation of joy.
The Sūtra says: "World-Honored One!

Sixteenth, seeking instruction.

Seventeenth, the realization of the path.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, there is a person whose body is wondrously vast," and so forth.
Eighteenth, the supreme seeking of the stage of Buddhahood.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti! If a bodhisattva should say:
'I adorn the Buddha-lands.'"
"One who is thus is not called a bodhisattva," and so forth.
Those abodes, in brief, are of eight kinds and are thus complete:

first, the abode of gathering; second, the abode of pure perfections; third, the abode of aspiration; fourth, the abode free from obstacles; fifth, the abode of the purified mind; sixth, the ultimate abode; seventh, the vast abode; and eighth, the profound abode.
Among these, the basis of inclusion is the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
The basis of pure dwelling in the perfections (*pāramitā*) is practice associated with the perfections.
The basis of aspiration is the desire to attain the form body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
The dwelling place free from obstacles refers to the remaining twelve types.
The dwelling place of the pure mind refers to the realization of the Path.
The ultimate dwelling place refers to the higher pursuit of the Buddha-ground.
Regarding the "vast and profound abodes," these apply to all abodes.
Within the first abode, when it is said, "A bodhisattva should give rise to such a thought:
'All sentient beings... and so forth, this constitutes the vast.
Furthermore, it is said: "If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a sentient being," and so forth;
this is profound. Within the second dwelling place, if it is said: "The bodhisattva does not dwell upon things while practicing generosity," and so forth; this is profound.
Furthermore, if it is further stated that "the mass of merit he possesses is inconceivable," and so forth, this refers to its vastness.
In this way, within other dwelling places, one should understand that vastness, profundity, and so on correspond accordingly.
The dwelling places have already been explained.
Fourth, regarding the antidotes: when one practices in those dwelling places through such corresponding modes of conduct, two kinds of antidotes should be known:
first, wrong practice; second, right practice associated with views.
In this context, "seeing" refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the first stage of dwelling, if it is said, "A bodhisattva should give rise to such a thought:
'All sentient beings... and so forth, this is the remedy for wrong practice—namely, that giving rise to such a thought constitutes a wrong practice on the part of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if it is said, "If a bodhisattva has the notion of a sentient being," and so forth, this refers to the counteractive practice for common views.
Such conceptual attachments must also be severed by the bodhisattva, namely the thought: "I should bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa."

In the context of the second stage of abiding, if it is said that "one should practice generosity," this refers to the remedy for wrong conduct; it does not mean that generosity itself is wrong conduct for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if it is said, "abiding in things" and so forth, this refers to the antidote for common views regarding correct practice.
Such conceptual attachments must also be severed by the bodhisattva; that is to say, because [the thought] arises, "I should practice generosity."
5. Regarding "non-loss," it means being free from the two extremes.
What are the two extremes?
They are the extreme of superimposition and the extreme of denial.
If one conceptually grasps at an intrinsic nature within phenomena that are merely conventional expressions, this is the extreme of superimposition;
if one grasps at the absence of self in phenomena as being non-existent, this is the extreme of deprecation.
In this context, if it is said, "O Bhagavān,
if the mass of merit is not a mass," this negates the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*), because that mass of merit lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as a conceptual construction.

Furthermore, if it is said, "For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of a 'mass of merit' (puṇyaskandha)," this excludes the extreme of nihilism (*apavāda*). For although that [merit] does not exist as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) according to its verbal expression, there is nevertheless a referent that can be spoken of; since the Tathāgata speaks of a mass of merit, it is thus demonstrated.
“Subhūti! As for ‘the Buddha-dharmas, the Buddha-dharmas,’ the Tathāgata has said they are not Buddha-dharmas”; this negates the extreme of superimposition (samāropa).
“They are called Buddha-dharmas”; this negates the extreme of denial (apavāda).
In this context, the statement "The Tathāgata says they are not Buddha-dharmas" reveals the meaning of non-loss;
the statement "These are called Buddha-dharmas" reveals the meaning of correspondence.
What is this correspondence?

If the Buddha-dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as they are described, then the Tathāgata would not have taught the Buddha-dharmas; for even without teaching them, one would know them for oneself. Therefore, they possess no intrinsic nature;
it is only for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that the Tathāgata speaks of them by the name "Buddha-dharmas."
In this manner, it should be understood that at all points the meaning of the unique [qualities] and their correspondence is revealed.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the Buddha-dharma comprises the matters of the perfections (pāramitā) as well as the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) such as the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Because the Bodhisattva is free from these two extremes, they no longer lose their respective antidotes; therefore, it is called "non-loss.

Sixth, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three types of stages: the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*), the stage of pure mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*), and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).

Among these, the first sixteen stages demonstrate the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*); the stage of abiding in the realization of the path is the stage of the pure mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*); and the subsequent [stages] represent the upward-seeking for the Buddha-ground.

Seventh, regarding the establishment of the title: as for the name "The Vajra that Can Sever," one should understand that this name possesses two meanings, corresponding to what is taught as entering the practice of right view and entering the practice of false view.
"Vajra" means subtle and firm. "Subtle" refers to being the cause of wisdom;
"firm" refers to being indestructible.

As for "that which can sever": within the *prajñāpāramitā*, that which is severed through hearing, reflection, and cultivation is severed just as a diamond cuts through its object; therefore, it is called the "diamond-like capacity to sever."
Furthermore, it is like the drawing of a vajra shape, which is broad at the beginning and the end, but narrow in the middle.

In this way, within the Prajñāpāramitā, that which is "narrow" refers to the Stage of Pure Mind (śuddhacittabhūmi); that which is "broad at the beginning and the end" refers to the Stage of Practice through Faith (adhimukticaryābhūmi) and the Stage of the Tathāgata (tathāgatabhūmi).
This demonstrates the meaning of the uncommon [teachings].
It should be understood that those five types of semantic categories are based on a progressive hierarchy, for they are all said to be based upon the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location.
Having finished his meal, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and as usual spread out his seat; sitting cross-legged with his body erect, he remained there unmoving in right mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

Then, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat in the midst of the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and stood respectfully, addressing the Buddha:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, well protects and attends to all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
The Treatise says:
The body of the Sūtra continues; the meaning and phrasing of this shall now be explained.
For what reason does the World-Honored One sit with the dignified deportment of one who is tranquil?
It is to demonstrate that only those who are tranquil are able to awaken to and expound the Dharma.

When the Sūtra speaks of "the well-gathered foremost Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas," it refers to mature Bodhisattvas who, at the time when the Buddha realizes perfect enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma, are established within the Bodhisattva-dharma through five kinds of meanings.
Because bodhisattvas possess seven kinds of greatness, this great assembly of beings is called *mahāsattva*.
What are the seven kinds of greatness?

First, greatness of the dharma; second, greatness of mind; third, greatness of faith and understanding; fourth, greatness of the pure mind; fifth, greatness of the provisions; sixth, greatness of time; and seventh, greatness of the fruition, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Regarding all bodhisattvas, what constitutes excellent gathering (*saṃgraha*)?
What is the foremost? That which accords with benefit and happiness is the excellent gathering that is foremost; it should be known to have six aspects:
First, time; second, differentiation; third, loftiness; fourth, solidity; fifth, pervasiveness; sixth, distinct characteristics. What is time?

Because they pertain to both present phenomena and the future, within that which is well-comprised by those bodhisattvas, "pleasure" refers to present phenomena and "benefit" refers to the future life.
What is the distinction between them?
Because it is distinguished by its superior inclusion of both mundane meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and supramundane noble ones such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is its greatness?
Because this wholesome gathering is unsurpassed.
What is its firmness?
It is its ultimate nature.
What is its universality?
It is the spontaneous and skillful gathering [of merit] within one's own and others' bodies.
What is its distinct characteristic?
Because it is superior among the means of skillfully gathering bodhisattvas who have not yet attained purity, the Sūtra speaks of the "first entrustment.
This is because those bodhisattvas and others who have already attained skillful gathering likewise establish [the teaching] through those five meanings at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
What is the first entrustment?
It consists of six kinds of causes and conditions:
first, the point of entry; second, acquisition through the nature of things (*dharmatā*); third, the transmission of teaching; fourth, non-loss; fifth, compassion; and sixth, reverence.
What is the point of entry?
It is because of being well-entrusted by a virtuous friend.
What is the natural law (*dharmatā*)?
Having already attained skillful means for gathering [disciples], that bodhisattva naturally gathers others through those very means.
What is "transmitting the instruction"?
It is saying, "You, too, should skillfully gather other bodhisattvas"; this is called transmitting the instruction.
These three types should be understood as, respectively, non-forgetfulness, compassion, and respect.
These two—skillful gathering and entrustment—demonstrate that the spiritual lineage is not interrupted.
The Sūtra says:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, within the Mahāyāna, resolve their mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
How should one dwell?
How should one practice?
How should one subdue the mind?
At that time, the Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
As you have said:
"The Tathāgata skillfully protects and cares for all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
As for a bodhisattva in the Mahāyāna who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should abide in this manner, practice in this manner, and subdue their mind in this manner.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, it is so.”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Commentary says:
This is the second section below, which initiates the mode of practice.
For what reason does the Elder Subhūti inquire?

There are six causes and conditions: first, to sever doubt; second, to give rise to faith and understanding; third, to enter into the profound meaning; fourth, to ensure non-retrogression; fifth, to engender joy; and sixth, to ensure that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
This is also precisely the Prajñāpāramitā that causes the lineage of the Buddhas not to be severed.
How does it cause the lineage of the Buddhas not to be severed?
It is because those who have doubts attain their severance.
There are bodhisattvas who possess merit and virtue but whose minds are not yet matured; they develop faith and understanding in the *prajñāpāramitā* upon hearing that it yields great merit.
Those whose minds are already matured enter into its profound meaning.
Those who have attained a state beyond being disparaged, through their zeal for upholding and practicing it, possess manifold virtues and no longer regress.
Those who have already attained compliance, integration, and a pure mind enter the Dharma spontaneously and experience joy upon seeing it;
furthermore, they are able to cause the Mahāyāna teachings to endure for a long time in future ages.
To state it briefly:

it is for the purpose of causing those who doubt to see [the truth]; for the purpose of gathering those who delight in merit and those bodhisattvas who have already reached maturity; for the purpose of causing those who have not been treated with contempt to apply themselves with diligence; and for the purpose of causing those who have attained a pure mind to rejoice.
When the Sūtra says, "How should one abide? it refers to aspiration and resolve;
when it says, "One should practice," it refers to the meditative absorption (samāpatti) of union;
when it says, "One should subdue the mind," it refers to the suppression of distraction.
Among these, "desire" (*chanda*) is the actual seeking;
"aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*) is the mental attention directed toward that which is sought.
"Concordant samāpatti" refers to non-conceptual *samādhi*.
Regarding the subduing of distraction: if the mind of that *samāpatti* becomes scattered, one restrains it and causes it to dwell [in concentration] once more.
The first [verse] demonstrates the path of gathering; the second demonstrates the path of accomplishment; and the third demonstrates the path of non-loss.
Why is it that he asks only about setting forth on the bodhisattva vehicle?
It is because of the distinctions among the three types of enlightenment.
Since this is a skillful question, one should address the Venerable Subhūti as follows:
"Excellent! The Sūtra says:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“Bodhisattvas give rise to this thought:

‘All sentient beings, as comprised within the realm of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—all sentient beings included within the realm of sentient beings—I shall lead them all into *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.’”
"In this way, although immeasurable and boundless sentient beings are brought to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this so, Subhūti?"
If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is it not so? Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not called a bodhisattva.
The Commentary says:
From this point downward is the third section on the dwelling places of practice; it extends to the end of the sutra and consists of eighteen gates, as fully explained previously.
Among these, the first clarifies the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*).

The scriptural statement, "all sentient beings, those comprised within the category of sentient beings," is a general description; the mention of "those born from eggs" and so forth is a specific description.
Furthermore, one should understand the distinctions categorized by birth, support, and objective sphere:
those born from eggs up to those born by transformation represent the distinction of birth;
whether they possess form or are formless represents the distinction of support.
Whether they possess perception, lack perception, or possess neither perception nor non-perception, these are distinguished by what is encompassed within their respective spheres (*viṣaya*).
As for those included within the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), this refers to the various abodes of sentient beings with diverse perceptions as established and taught by the Buddha.
Regarding the statement, "I shall cause all to enter nirvana without remainder," why is this unattainable goal aspired to?
There is no fault, for it is encompassed by birth; since all [beings] are indeed born.

As it has been stated, because birth from eggs and the other modes of birth are all included within the category of vows, those born from eggs, moisture, the non-percipient beings, and those who are neither percipient nor non-percipient are unable [to fulfill them].
How can one cause all sentient beings to enter nirvana?
There are three causes and conditions:

first, those born in difficult circumstances obtain the opportune time; second, those born in non-difficult circumstances who have not yet matured are brought to maturity; and third, those already matured are liberated.
Why is it that the "nirvana-element without remainder" is spoken of, rather than simply "nirvana"?
If it were stated directly as such, it would not differ from the "expedient nirvana" of the first dhyāna and so forth, which was taught by the Blessed One.
Because they rely on their own power as great men (*puruṣa*), they attain it even in the absence of a Buddha, yet it is not ultimate.
Why, then, is it not called the realm of *nirvāṇa* with remainder?
Because it is a shared fruit; they attain this fruit through their own past karma and by encountering the teachings of a Buddha.
Furthermore, it is not exclusively physical suffering that remains.

Thus, because *nirvāṇa* and *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* are the fruits of human effort, are common fruits, are not ultimate fruits, and are not exclusive fruits, they are therefore said to be "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "Thus, immeasurable sentient beings have entered nirvāṇa," this demonstrates that each of the modes of birth, such as birth from an egg and so forth, is individually immeasurable.
As for the statement "There are no sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa," what is its meaning?
Just as when a bodhisattva attains nirvāṇa for themselves, there are no separate sentient beings.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva.
What is the meaning of this?
If a bodhisattva conceives of sentient beings as "other" rather than as their own self, they cannot be called a bodhisattva. Why is that?

"If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*), the notion of a person (*pudgala-saṃjñā*), or the notion of a life-span (*jīva-saṃjñā*), they are not called a 'bodhisattva'.
What is the meaning of this?

If one revolves with the grasping of the notions of a sentient being, a life-span, or a person due to afflictions (*kleśa*), then one possesses the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) and the notion of a sentient being revolves within those very sentient beings.

Once the bodhisattva has ceased to revolve therein, because he has severed the view of self, he attains the practice of self-conduct—meaning he realizes the mark of equality in the conduct of the five aggregates—and thus gains faith and understanding in the equality of self and others.
That Bodhisattva is not a sentient being, a life-principle, a person, or a grasper—this is its meaning.
Furthermore, when the sutra says, "The Bodhisattvas give rise to such a mind," and so forth, it demonstrates the aspiration and vow for the Bodhisattva to abide in this manner.
"If a bodhisattva has the notion of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva" indicates the time when one should practice in accordance with the samāpatti of such cultivation.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, they are not called a bodhisattva; this demonstrates that one should thus subdue the mind when it is distracted during the time of its gathering.

Just as when a bodhisattva emerges from a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that is in accordance with reality, the notion of a "sentient being" no longer arises, because they abide in the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, there is no sentient being who attains nirvāṇa; rather, this attainment is the fulfillment of those aspirations and vows which, among all states of abiding, are the most supreme. This is because when one practices the modes of conduct associated with that [realization] while in other states of abiding, one will certainly attain it by relying upon those aspirations and vows.
The meaning of this desire and aspiration need not be explained further.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

One practices giving without dwelling on things; one practices giving without dwelling anywhere. One does not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor does one dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not dwelling on the perception of signs. Why is that?
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, the mass of their merit is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think?
“Can the eastern void be measured? Subhūti replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “It is so.”
“Subhūti! Can the empty space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below be measured? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs, the mass of merit is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner alone.
The Commentary says:
Below this is the second [section], the practice associated with the perfections (*pāramitā*).
From this point onward, in the remaining sections, it should be understood that there are five ways of explaining according to their respective associations:
first, based on the meaning; second, the explanation of characteristics; third, inclusion; fourth, establishment; and fifth, manifestation.
The dwelling place serves as the basis for the counteractive;
that very dwelling place constitutes the characteristic of the teaching;
and aspiration serves as the means of upholding it.
The primary meaning of "abiding" is for the purpose of establishment;
its manifestation consists of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with the mind and the gathering of a distracted mind.

Within the context of the pure abiding in the perfections (*pāramitā*), the Sūtra states: "A bodhisattva practices generosity without dwelling on things. This is based on the ultimate meaning, as it demonstrates the remedy for dwelling in attachment.
The Sūtra states, "One should practice giving"; this is a statement regarding its characteristics, for the six pāramitās encompass the essential nature of all *dāna*.
There are three kinds of *dāna*:
first, the gift of material requisites (*upakaraṇa-dāna*), which refers to the *dānapāramitā*.
The second, the gift of fearlessness, refers to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);

the third, the gift of the Dharma, refers to the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), and so forth.
If one lacks diligence, then when preaching the Dharma to those who receive it, one will be unable to do so due to weariness.

If one lacks meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), then one will preach the Dharma with a defiled mind because of craving for faith, respect, and offerings, and because of being unable to endure the afflictions of cold and heat.
If one lacks wisdom, one will explain the Dharma erroneously, which entails many faults;
thus, it is impossible to accomplish the gift of Dharma without these three.
Those various *pāramitās* have two kinds of fruits, namely those of the future and the present.
Regarding future fruits: through the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one obtains great rewards of merit;
through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), one obtains a perfect body, such as that of Śakra or Brahmā;
and through the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), one obtains great assistance and a large retinue.
Through the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one attains the non-interruption of the fruits of maturation;
through the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), one attains an invulnerable physical body;
and through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), one attains sharp and keen faculties, manifold joys, and mastery among the assembly of great beings.
The present fruit consists of obtaining all forms of faith, respect, and offerings, as well as nirvana in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).

Within this context, if a bodhisattva practices giving for the sake of seeking a future fruit, they practice giving while dwelling upon the objective basis (*vastu*); as such, they would receive back the very same kind of object as that which was given. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One practices giving without dwelling upon the objective basis."

If one practices giving for the sake of seeking future fruits such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is practicing giving with a basis of dwelling; therefore, the Sūtra says, "One should practice giving without dwelling on anything."
The fruits of *śīla* (ethical discipline) and so forth are manifold; because they cannot be individually distinguished, they are collectively termed "having a dwelling.

If one seeks present fruits—such as faith, reverence, and making offerings—one practices giving while dwelling in form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore, the Sūtra says, "not dwelling in form," and so forth.

If one practices giving for the sake of attaining nirvana in the present life, it is practicing giving while dwelling in phenomena; therefore, the sutra says, "One should practice giving without dwelling in phenomena."
Furthermore, when the sūtra says "one should practice giving," it refers to the grasping of the aspiration for giving.
When the sūtra says "one practices giving without abiding," this non-abiding is for the purpose of establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within this context, because of non-abiding, it demonstrates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāva*), wherein the fact that things do not abide is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

When the Sūtra says, "A bodhisattva should practice giving in this way, not abiding in the perception of signs (*nimitta-saṃjñā*)," this is intended to demonstrate that during both the time of the samādhi associated with [signs] and the time of gathering back a distracted mind, one does not abide in the perception of signs.
Having thus established non-abiding, there may be some bodhisattvas who, because they crave merit, are unable to endure this.
To enable them to endure it, the World-Honored One reveals that the mass of merit from practicing giving without abiding is as vast as space, due to three causes and conditions:
first, it pervades all places, meaning that merit arises within both the states of abiding and non-abiding.
Second, because it is exceptionally vast, expansive, and sublime;
third, because it is inexhaustible, ultimate, and without end.

Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows all these sentient beings; the Tathāgata fully sees all these sentient beings. Subhūti!

Therefore, the Sūtra says, "There are those who uphold the precepts, cultivate merit, and possess wisdom"; these three trainings—superior morality and so forth—demonstrate the qualities of spiritual practice.

Beginning with virtues such as fewness of desires, up to the attainment of samādhi and so forth—the Sūtra states, "Having already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, up to having single-minded pure faith," and so on; this demonstrates the accumulation of causes.
If even those who possess single-minded pure faith attain such [results], how much more so for those who give rise to the perception of reality?
When the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings," this demonstrates being embraced by a virtuous friend.
"Knowing" refers to knowing the collection of names (nāmakāya).
"Seeing" refers to seeing the collection of forms (rūpakāya).
This means that within all activities of walking and staying, one knows the mind and sees its basis.
Regarding the scriptural statement that "one generates and takes up an immeasurable mass of merit," this demonstrates the inclusion of meritorious virtue.
"Generates" refers to the time when merit is properly arising;
"takes up" refers to the retention of its seeds at the time of that merit's cessation.

The Sūtra states: "These bodhisattvas no longer have the notion of a self or the notion of a sentient being," up to: "If a bodhisattva has the notion of a dharma, they are immediately attached to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span. This demonstrates the notion of reality (*bhūtasaṃjñā*) as the remedy for the five kinds of false grasping.
What are the five types of false grasping? First, non-Buddhists;

second, ordinary worldlings and śrāvakas within the Buddha's teaching; third, bodhisattvas with overweening pride; fourth, the worldly meditative attainment of cessation of perception; and fifth, the meditative attainment of non-perception.
The first is the transformation of the notion of self.
The second is the transformation of the characteristics of phenomena.
The third is the transformation of the notion of non-purity; this still involves the grasping of phenomena.
That which possesses the grasping of dharmas refers to the grasping of non-existent dharmas.
The fourth is the transformation of perception;
the fifth is the transformation of non-perception.

These bodhisattvas do not engage in any of those [notions]; herein it is clearly revealed that they possess ethical discipline and so forth, up to the point that they shall generate immeasurable masses of merit.

As for the sūtra’s question, "For what reason?", this refers to the erroneous grasping within this context: only the notions of "dharma" and "adharma" arise, but not the notion of "self," because the notion of a self and its underlying basis do not arise.

However, because the latent tendencies within the notion of a self (ātman-saṃjñā) have not been severed, there is the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha). Therefore, the Sūtra states: "If these bodhisattvas grasp at the notion of dharmas, they are attached to the grasping at a self"; and "If the notion of non-dharmas arises, they still possess the grasping at a self," and so forth.
Within this transformation of the notion of "self" (*ātma-saṃjñā*), other meanings have yet to be explained.

Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “If a bodhisattva has the notion of dharmas, he is attached to a self,” and so forth: therein, one takes the characteristic of one’s own substantial continuity as the notion of "self"; that which is grasped as "mine" is the notion of "sentient being" (*sattva-saṃjñā*); taking what lasts from birth until death as the notion of "life-force" (*jīva-saṃjñā*); and it should be understood that taking [the aggregates] successively in other realms of existence is the notion of "person" (*pudgala-saṃjñā*).

In this context, the statement "one should produce the thought of reality" should be understood as referring to the meaning (*artha*), because it demonstrates the antidote to the thought of unreality.

The phrase "within these words and phrases of the sūtra" refers to the mode of expression (*vyañjana*), because it demonstrates that the Dharma-body consists of speech; thus, one should produce the thought of reality regarding those very [words].
The statement "should be born" refers to being sustained by aspiration and desire.
The phrase "these bodhisattvas no longer have the transformation of the notion of self" and so forth establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

"Subhūti! One should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one not grasp at dharmas. This is a clear exposition; it means that during both the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) associated with [the path] and the state of the distracted mind, "one should not grasp at dharmas" refers to not making any conceptual discrimination regarding either the essence of dharmas or the selflessness of dharmas.
Furthermore, regarding the essential meaning of the teaching on the Dharma-body, a sutra states:
"For this reason, the Tathāgata has always taught the Dharma-gate of the raft parable: if one understands this, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
"Therefore, even dharmas should be relinquished, because the notion of reality arises;
how much more so non-dharmas, as they are logically untenable.
This brief explanation demonstrates that a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the dharma-body of speech should not form notions of unreality.

Because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are named 'Noble Ones' (*ārya*). Here, "unconditioned" means the absence of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*); therefore, Bodhisattvas who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) receive this name.

Within the state of non-arising and non-activity, the Tathāgata’s transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is termed "purity"; therefore, the Tathāgata is designated as one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Among these, the first meaning of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is because it is manifested during meditative equipoise (samāpatti) and when distracting thoughts are suppressed.

From here below is the fifth [section], which concerns the absence of pride when attaining excellence through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*).

As previously summarized, there are eight types of dwelling places; those listed below, totaling twelve, should be understood as the remedies for the dwelling places characterized by the separation from obstacles.

fourth, not practicing the path with minor objects of focus and mental attention yet abandoning sentient beings.

10. although able to endure suffering, one lacks the provisions for wisdom; 11. although possessing the provisions for wisdom, one does not exercise self-restraint;
