"If a bodhisattva were to speak thus:"
“‘I adorn the Buddha-lands,’ that bodhisattva speaks an untruth. Why is this? Because...”
Subhūti! That which the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely designated as the "adornment of Buddha-fields. Therefore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind while abiding nowhere: they should not give rise to a mind by abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind by abiding in sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; they should give rise to that mind while abiding nowhere.
The Commentary states:
Below this is the seventh section, concerning the vow to purify the Buddha-field.

Among the twelve types of practices for departing from obstacles, this is for the purpose of cultivating the path by forming mental attention free from minor objects of focus; thus the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"If a bodhisattva should say:
'I adorn the Buddha-lands,' and so forth.

If one contemplates the adornment and purification of the lands, one then discriminates among phenomena such as form and develops attachment to them. To avoid this, the Sūtra says: "Therefore, Subhūti!"
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind without abiding anywhere—not abiding in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena," and so forth.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! For example, suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains.”
Subhūti, what do you think? Is this body large?
Subhūti said: “It is exceedingly great,
World-Honored One!”
Why is this? The Buddha has said that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
That body is a non-body; it is for this reason it is called the "Great Body."
The Commentary states:
From here below is the eighth [section], for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Among the twelve types of abandoning obstacles, in order to abandon the abandonment of sentient beings, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"For example, there is a person whose body is like Sumeru, the king of mountains," and so forth.
What does this demonstrate?
It is for the sake of maturing sentient beings in the desire realm.
Even the great bodies of all those such as the Asura King Rāhu, which are as vast as Mount Sumeru, should not even be seen in their own substance, let alone others.
The Sūtra’s statement that “the Tathāgata says it is not a substantial entity” reveals the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya);
the statement that “that entity is a non-entity” reveals that the essence of phenomena is without arising and without activity.
This demonstrates the intrinsic nature, the characteristics, and the distinctions [of the aggregates].
The Sūtra says:
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges. What do you think?
[Would there be many such rivers?]”
"Would these grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be many? Subhūti replied, "Very many."
“World-Honored One!
The Ganges Rivers alone are already countless; how much more so their sands?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! I now speak to you in truth.

If there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers, and gave them as a gift to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.”
Subhūti, what do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Subhūti said: “It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"That son of good family or daughter of good family will acquire exceedingly great merit. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
If one were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift;

yet if a son or daughter of good family, from this Dharma-door, were to even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it to others, this merit would surpass the former merit by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

In whatever place this Dharma-gate, even as little as a four-line verse, is taught, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra! Subhūti,
you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma.
"Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, or one who is as worthy of respect as a Buddha.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this Dharma-gate be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This Dharma door is named 'Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā. By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that?
Subhūti! That which the Buddha calls the perfection of wisdom is, in fact, not the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
There is no dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
The Commentary says:
The following ninth section is for the purpose of distancing oneself from the distraction of conforming to external treatises.

Among the twelve types of obstacles to be abandoned, in order to distance oneself from the distraction of delighting in external treatises, the Sūtra sets forth four kinds of causal conditions to demonstrate the superiority and excellence of this Dharma:
first, the accumulation of merit; second, the offerings of devas and others; third, the performance of what is difficult to do; and fourth, the arousal of mindfulness toward the Tathāgata and others.
The sūtra states, “Subhūti!
As many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges River,” and so forth; this refers to the accumulation of merit.
The sūtra states, “Subhūti!”... [and so on].
The passage beginning with "In whatever place this Dharma-gate is preached... refers to the offerings made by devas and others.
The passage from the Sūtra beginning with "Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost rarity... refers to what is difficult to perform.
Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "Wherever this sūtra may be located," etc., it gives rise to the mindfulness of the Tathāgata and others.
Within this context, "one who speaks" refers to one who speaks directly for the sake of others, while "one who transmits" refers to one who instructs others;
thus, having demonstrated the excellence of this method as a superior remedy against the distraction of delighting in external treatises.

Within such teachings, one might give rise to the attachment of grasping at the meaning according to the literal expression; in order to counteract that future fault, the Sūtra states: "The Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddha is not [in fact] Prajñāpāramitā."
Just as the perfection of wisdom is not a perfection, so too there is no other dharma that the Tathāgata has taught.
To clarify this meaning, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?

Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? This reveals the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of the dharma-gate of both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of equality (*samatā-lakṣaṇa*).
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied,
“Those atoms are exceedingly many.”
“World-Honored One!
“Subhūti! These atoms spoken of by the Tathāgata are not atoms; they are called 'atoms' [only] by name.”
“The Tathāgata speaks of the world, yet it is not a world; it is merely called ‘the world.
The Commentary states:
From here below, the tenth section clarifies the Middle Way analysis that refutes the associated formations within the grasping of matter and the bodies of sentient beings.
Among the twelve types of abandonment regarding the obstacles, in order to abandon the lack of skillful means regarding mastery over the marks of images, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Regarding all the atoms within the trichiliocosm," and so forth. Those [atoms] are immeasurable;
because the bodhisattva who practices by taking objects as mental focal points constantly takes the world as a focal point for his practice, it is called the "trichiliocosm."
Within this, in order to dismantle the characteristic of the reflected image of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*) are revealed:
first, the skillful means of subtle analysis, as in the passage beginning, "Would all the atoms (*paramāṇu*) in the three-thousandfold world system be many? and so forth.
Second, the non-contemplation of skillful means, as the Sūtra says: "These atoms, the Tathāgata says they are not atoms; they are called 'atoms'.
This is for the purpose of destroying the mark of the reflected image of sentient beings' bodies, as the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks of a world; it is not a world; it is called a 'world'."
Within this, "world" (*loka*) refers to the world of sentient beings; it is designated as the "world of sentient beings" solely by means of the body of names (*nāmakāya*).
Not dwelling upon the skillful means of the body of names is precisely what reveals the destruction of that reflected image, and no further subtle methods of composition are discussed.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
“The Tathāgata has spoken of the thirty-two marks of a great man; these are indeed no-marks, and are merely named ‘the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the eleventh section, clarifying the offering and service rendered to the Tathāgata.
Among the twelve types of obstacles to be abandoned, in order to abandon the lack of the provisions for merit, the Sūtra asks, "What do you think?

Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man? This demonstrates that when one approaches and makes offerings to the Tathāgata for the sake of the provisions for merit, one should not perceive the Tathāgata merely through the perfection of his physical marks.
How should one see it?
One should see it as the dharmakāya of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The Sūtra says:
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in acts of giving."

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, from within this Dharma-door, even receives and upholds as little as a four-line verse and explains it to others, their merit will be exceedingly great—immeasurable and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).

At that time, when Subhūti heard this sutra being preached, he deeply understood its meaning and intent; shedding tears and weeping with grief, he wiped away his tears and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, Bhagavān!"

"How rare, Sugata! Regarding this most profound Dharma-gate spoken by the Buddha, from the time of my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate."
"Why is this? Subhūti! That which the Buddha calls the perfection of wisdom is, in truth, not the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!

If there should be anyone who hears this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they will give rise to the mark of reality; you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.”
World-Honored One!
This true mark is actually no mark; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "true mark," "true mark.
World-Honored One!
That I have now been able to hear such a Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.
However, if in a future age there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, those people will be the most rare and extraordinary of all.
Why is this? Because this person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span. Why is this?
The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks.
Why is this? Because one who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is.
If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is most rare.”

Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not a foremost pāramitā; it is because the Tathāgata calls it the foremost pāramitā, and those immeasurable Buddhas also speak of it as a pāramitā, that it is named the foremost pāramitā.
The Commentary states:
From here below is the twelfth [section], which concerns the distancing oneself from gain, fatigue, and feverish affliction so as not to give rise to lack of diligence or regression, and so forth.
Among the twelve types of obstacles to be abandoned, in order to distance oneself from the savoring of indolence, gain, and other such pleasures, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"If there are good sons or good daughters who give away their body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," and so forth.
In this context, the body experiences fatigue and the mind experiences feverish affliction; by means of these two, one either retreats from or fails to initiate that diligence.
What does this demonstrate? It shows that even though one has sacrificed such a body, one's own merit does not equal this merit;
how then can a single body, through the attachment to indolence and the like, act as an obstacle?
Why did the Elder Subhūti shed tears and say, "I have never before heard such Dharma-gates as these"?
It is because he heard that this supreme merit is so vast that it exceeds the merit of giving away immeasurable bodies, and no other superior merit need be mentioned.

If, upon hearing of such supreme merit, one arouses diligence and conceives of this Dharma as being according to its true meaning, then—in order to eliminate this fault—the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, if there be anyone who hears this sūtra and their faith becomes pure, they will give rise to the mark of reality; you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit," and so forth.
Within this very reality (*tathatā*), in order to eliminate conceptualization regarding that reality, the Sūtra states: "That which is reality is itself non-reality," and so forth.
The Sūtra says: "World-Honored One!
That I have now heard such a Dharma-gate and am able to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

But if, in a future age, there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and are able to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, such people would be the most rare and extraordinary. What is the meaning of this?
In order to inspire a sense of shame and remorse in those bodhisattvas who are attached to gain and offerings and who exceed in indolence, [the Buddha said]:

"When the True Dharma is extinguished in the future, there will still be bodhisattvas who uphold this Dharma-gate; thus, they have no grasping at persons (*pudgala-grāha*) nor grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Why, then, do you not feel shame and remorse for abandoning practice while the True Dharma is flourishing?"

The Sūtra’s statement that “this person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span” demonstrates the absence of grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*);
the statement that “the mark of self is not a mark,” and so forth, demonstrates the absence of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
The Sūtra states, "For what reason?
Because being free from all marks is precisely what is called 'the Buddhas,'" which demonstrates the characteristics of the Bodhisattvas' compliant training:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are free from all marks; therefore, we too should train in this same way."
These scriptural passages are taught for the purpose of preventing the regression of diligence.
Within them, the phrase "whether by discrimination or by resolute belief" explains the preceding term through the subsequent one.
"Receiving" means receiving the words;
"upholding" means upholding the meaning.

Because one would otherwise fail to initiate diligence, the Sūtra says, "If there be anyone who hears this sūtra and is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid," and so forth; for it is through such states as being startled that one fails to initiate diligence.
Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Blessed One taught that phenomena exist and that emptiness exists; yet when hearing this sūtra, they are startled because they hear that phenomena do not exist,
terrified because they hear that emptiness does not exist,
and fearful because, when reflecting upon it, they cannot reconcile these two points of non-existence.
There is another interpretation: it should be understood that this is because there are three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
That is to say, because of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), arising (*utpatti*), and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As the Sūtra says: "For what reason?"
"Subhūti! When the Tathāgata speaks of the 'foremost pāramitā,' it is not a foremost pāramitā.
What is the meaning of this?
Furthermore, because it explains the second basis for the arising of shame and remorse, it says:
"This dharma is thus supreme; you should not be negligent.
Within this context, because it is superior among the other pāramitās, it is called the first pāramitā.

Furthermore, when the Sūtra states, "That which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is also called a pāramitā by immeasurable Buddhas," this statement reveals that all Buddhas unanimously proclaim it as the foremost; therefore, it is named the foremost.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! What the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is, in truth, not the perfection of patience.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

When I was formerly cut and mangled in body by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a person, and no perception of a life-span; there was neither form nor the absence of form.
Why is this? Subhūti,

when my limbs were being severed joint by joint in the past, if I had possessed the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

Subhūti! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience; during all those lifetimes, there was no perception of a self, no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a person, and no perception of a life-span.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling.

One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
Therefore, the Buddha said that the bodhisattva’s mind does not dwell on form when practicing giving. Subhūti,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
The marks of all sentient beings are, in fact, no-marks.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all sentient beings are, in truth, not sentient beings. “Subhūti!
The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, who speaks reality, who speaks according to things as they are, and who does not speak otherwise. Subhūti,
regarding the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him, there is neither reality nor falsehood.
Subhūti! It is as if a person enters the darkness and sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva dwells upon phenomena while practicing giving, it is just like this.
Subhūti! It is as if a person with eyes, when the night has ended and the light of the sun shines forth, sees various forms.
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on things, it is also like this.
The Commentary says:
Below this is the thirteenth [section], which clarifies the endurance of suffering.
Among the twelve types [of practices] based on being free from obstacles, in order to abandon the inability to endure suffering, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"The Tathāgata speaks of the perfection of patience," and so forth.
Within this, there are two aspects:
first, the capacity for patience; second, the departure from the incapacity for patience.
There are three types of patience:
first, patience according to its object; second, the characteristics of patience; and third, patience by way of category.
Among these, by what characteristics does patience according to its object arise?
As shown by the distinctions in patience (*kṣānti*), it serves as the antidote to those causes and conditions.
What is that which is capable of enduring?
It is the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
How is this to be demonstrated?
As the Sūtra says: "That which the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is, in truth, not the perfection of patience.
How, then, should one understand the characteristics of patience?

When others direct ill will or the like toward oneself, because one lacks the notion of a self and so forth, one does not give rise to thoughts of anger; nor does one conceive the notion of existence regarding the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), nor the notion of non-existence regarding that which is not a perfection.
How is this demonstrated?
It is because the Sūtra says: "When I was once dismembered by King Kali, at that time I had no notion of a self," and "neither having marks nor being without marks," and so forth.
What is the patience of the category?
It is also of two kinds:
first, the patience toward extreme suffering; second, the patience toward continuous suffering.
How is this demonstrated?
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti, when my body was being dismembered limb by limb in the past, if there had been a notion of a self, anger and resentment would have arisen," and so forth.
What is the patience toward suffering in its continuity?
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience," and so forth.
Regarding the causes and conditions for not enduring [suffering], there are three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of saṃsāra; second, the suffering of conflict with sentient beings; and third, the suffering of lacking resources for enjoyment.

Within this, the Sūtra states: "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so forth; this is intended to demonstrate the remedy for the causes and conditions of the endurance of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Regarding those who would give rise to the bodhicitta, because of the three characteristics of suffering, they may be unwilling to do so;
therefore, it is said that one should abandon all marks (*nimitta*). Herein, "all marks" is used to reveal these three characteristics of suffering.

If one is attached to form and so forth, one will become exhausted within the suffering of saṃsāra and the bodhicitta will not arise; therefore, as previously stated, the Sūtra says, "One should not give rise to the mind while dwelling on form," and so on.
"Not abiding in non-dharmas" means that non-dharmas are selfless; because one does not abide in either non-dharmas or the selflessness of dharmas.
In order to accomplish those various forms of non-abiding, the Sūtra speaks by negating other matters, saying:
"One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere."
Why is this? If there is a mind that dwells, it is precisely non-dwelling, and so forth.
As the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."

"A Bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner," up to "all sentient beings are, in truth, no sentient beings. This demonstrates the patience that counteracts the suffering arising from the perception of sentient beings as real entities; it means practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*) for the sake of all sentient beings.
How could one possibly "give rise to anger" toward them?

Because one cannot be without sentient beings and the perception of sentient beings, due to these causes and conditions, one becomes weary when encountering opposition from sentient beings; therefore, [the teaching] demonstrates person-non-self (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomenon-non-self (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The Sūtra states: "Subhūti, the Tathāgata is a speaker of truth," and so forth. What does this demonstrate?
It is intended to enable one to endure [the teaching] by inspiring faith in the Tathāgata.
Among these, "speaking truthfully" is for the purpose of revealing the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
"speaking reality" is for the purpose of revealing that within the practice of conventional truth there are the characteristics of both affliction and purification.
Among these, "reality" (bhūta) refers to the fact that some of these practices involve affliction while others involve purification.
"Consistent with speech" (yathārtha) refers to its being the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
"Not inconsistent with speech" (aviparītārtha) refers to the fact that within the practice of the ultimate truth, there exist the characteristics of both affliction and purification.

Having spoken these words of true speech and so forth, because there is attachment arising within this very context regarding the nature of verbal expression, in order to dispel that, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"Because the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him are neither real nor false.
As for "neither real," it is because the nature of verbal expression does not exist.
"Non-delusion" means that things do not exist by way of their own nature as they are expressed in words.
The Sūtra says, "Subhūti, it is as if someone were to enter the darkness," and so forth; this demonstrates the antidote to the causes and conditions for enduring the suffering of lacking resources.
If one practices giving for the sake of karmic retribution, one becomes attached to phenomena while performing that renunciation.
Delighting in those things, one fails to understand the transcendence of sensual pleasures and painful feelings; it is like entering darkness, not knowing "where I am going."
His joy and desire for pleasure are likewise so.

If one practices giving without attachment to material things, it should be viewed as being like a man with sight who, when the night has passed and the sun has risen, sees various forms and proceeds wherever he wishes. It should be seen in this way.
When that night of ignorance has passed and the sun of wisdom has arisen, one perceives various objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) as they truly are.
Because they do not understand the escape from sensual pleasure and painful feeling, they take delight in sensual pleasure.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this Dharma-gate, then the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows these people, fully sees these people, and fully awakens to these people; they shall all achieve an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit."

“Subhūti! If there were good men or good women who, in the first part of the day, gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; in the middle part of the day, they again gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and in the latter part of the day, they again gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—thus relinquishing immeasurable bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas by means of bodily charity.

If there should be another person who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, believes with faith and does not slander it, their merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; how much more so for one who copies it down, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, practices it, and extensively explains it to others.
“Subhūti! To state it briefly, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
This Dharma-gate was taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, and explain it extensively for others, the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people; they shall all accomplish an inconceivable, incomparable, boundless, and immeasurable mass of merit.
Such persons as these, Subhūti, shall indeed bear the burden of the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Those who delight in inferior teachings will be unable to accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this sutra to others.

It is impossible for those who harbor views of a self, views of a sentient being, views of a person, or views of a life-span to accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this Dharma-gate to others.
“Subhūti! Wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the worlds—devas, humans, and asuras.”
"You should know that this place shall be as a stūpa; all should pay homage, circumambulate it with reverence, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, they will be treated with contempt by others. Why is this?

Because the karmic offenses of such a person from previous lives, which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms, are extinguished by the contempt shown by people in the present life; they shall thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, during immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I encountered eight thousand four hundred million *nayuta* hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas. I personally attended upon and made offerings to them all, none of whom I passed by in vain.”
Subhūti! Such immeasurable Buddhas as these, I have all personally served and made offerings to, none passing me by in vain.

If, moreover, there should be someone in a future age, at the end of time, who is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, the merit they obtain would be such that the merit from all the Buddhas whom I have made offerings to does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal a thousand-million-billionth part, nor can it be reached even by calculation or analogy.

“Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who, in a future age or at the end of the eon, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, were I to fully describe the merit they would obtain, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and confused, falling into doubt and lack of faith.”
"Subhūti! You should know that this Dharma-gate is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
The Commentary says:
Below this is the fourteenth [section], "Leaving Behind the Taste of Tranquility.
Among the twelve types of leaving behind obstacles, in order to leave behind the deficiency of the accumulations for wisdom, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Subhūti..."
"If there be good sons or good daughters who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this Dharma-gate," and so forth.
In this context, in order to eliminate the distractions of *samādhi*, five kinds of supreme merits associated with the Dharma are revealed:

first, being remembered and approached by the Tathāgata; second, the accumulation of merit; third, praise for the Dharma and its practice; fourth, offerings from devas and others; and fifth, the eradication of transgressions.
What is the Tathāgata’s mindful recollection and close attendance?
The sūtra says: "receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting," and so forth; "the Tathāgata knows them with Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata sees them with the Buddha-eye," and so forth.
Among these, "receiving" refers to the practice of recitation;
"retaining" refers to not being forgetful.
As for "reading" or "reciting," this explains the causes for receiving and retaining: one reads because one wishes to receive [the teachings], and one recites because one wishes to retain them.
Furthermore, "reading" refers to the practice of recitation;
"upholding" refers to comprehensively grasping the meaning.
What constitutes the gathering of merit?
The Sūtra says: "All shall attain the accomplishment of an immeasurable and boundless mass of merit," and so forth.
What is the praise for the Dharma and its practice?
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!"
To summarize, the passage beginning with "this sutra is inconceivable and immeasurable" constitutes a praise of the Dharma.
Within this, it is "inconceivable" because it is realized only through self-awakening.
"Inconceivable" means that there is nothing equal to it and nothing superior to it.

When the Sūtra states, "This Dharma-gate was taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle," this establishes the meaning of being inconceivable.
Among these, it should be understood that it is "supreme" because other vehicles cannot equal it, and "most excellent" because the afflictive obstructions and the cognitive obstructions are purified.
When the Sūtra says, "If there be anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sūtra, and explain it extensively for others," and so forth, this is a praise of its practice.
Within this, the statement that "the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision achieve an immeasurable mass of merit" is the general description;
"inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable" is the detailed explanation.
Such persons as these are those who bear the burden of the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; that is to say, they carry upon their shoulders the heavy responsibility of a bodhisattva.
When the Sūtra says, "Subhūti!

Those who delight in inferior dharmas will be unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this sūtra for others," it refers to those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The Sūtra states, "If there are those who hold the view of a self," up to "there is no possibility that they will receive and uphold [the teaching]," because these are individuals who possess the view of a self and sentient beings, yet claim for themselves the title of Bodhisattva.
What is meant by "the offerings of devas and others"? As the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, wherever this sūtra may be, it should be honored by all the world—devas, humans, and asuras," and so forth.

In this regard, because one makes offerings with flowers, garlands, incense for burning, perfumed incense, unguents, powdered incense, robes, parasols, banners, and flags, and because one pays homage, prostrates, and circumambulates it to the right, it is called a *caitya*.
What is the eradication of offenses?
It refers to what the Sūtra says: "If a good man or a good woman receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sūtra, they will be treated with contempt by others," and so forth.
This matter of humiliation has immeasurable aspects; to demonstrate these, the term "contempt" is used.
When the Sūtra says, "One shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," it is to demonstrate the eradication of transgressions.

Regarding what was previously stated—that by these causes and conditions one produces immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merit—one should now understand that the meaning of "immeasurable, incalculable" shall be explained.
"Powerful" means that it is intensely matured.
"Abundant" means that it is complete.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!"

The passage beginning with "I recall the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*, *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," and so forth, demonstrates his majestic power (*prabhāva*); that is to say, it is the majestic power of the mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*), because that mass of merit is exceedingly remote, lofty, and supreme.
In this context, "incalculable eons" (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa) should be understood as extending up until the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
"Beyond incalculable [eons]" means exceeding even that previous duration.
"Directly receiving" refers to making offerings.
"Non-futility" means that one never departs from making offerings.
As the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, in the future final age, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sūtra, were I to fully describe the merit they would obtain, some who hear it might have their minds become狂亂 (madly disturbed). Such passages demonstrate that because [the merit] is so vast, it may either serve as a cause for madness or result in a state of a distracted mind; this should be understood.
Who could possibly describe this power of that [Buddha] and its manifold qualities?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"One should know that this Dharma-gate is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
This is shown because the substance of that merit and its fruit cannot be measured.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How do they abide?
How do they practice?
"How does one subdue the mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to this thought:"
"I should bring all sentient beings to extinction, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Although I have thus brought all sentient beings to extinction, not a single sentient being has actually been extinguished."
Why is this? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti,
in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that can be called "a bodhisattva who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Commentary states:
Below this is the fifteenth section, on being free from the agitation of joy at the time of realizing the Path.
Among the twelve types of obstacles to be abandoned, in order to eliminate self-appropriation, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva generate the mind of enlightenment, abide in it, and practice it?
Why, then, was this initial question raised?
When a Bodhisattva is about to enter the realization of the Way, they personally perceive a state of superiority and think:
"Abiding thus, practicing thus, and subduing the mind thus, I shall bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa."

To counteract this, Subhūti asks how one should abide at that time, how one should practice, and how one should subdue the mind, to which the Blessed One replies with "one should give rise to such a mind," and so forth.
Furthermore, when the Sūtra says, "Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva [thinks] 'there are sentient beings,'" and so forth, it is to reveal the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) or its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If one says, "I am correctly practicing the Bodhisattva vehicle," this constitutes the grasping at a self.
To counteract that [misconception], the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever called 'a bodhisattva who has resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Subhūti replied to the Buddha, “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Bhagavān! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata obtained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had obtained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me.
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for this reason the Buddha Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me the prediction, speaking these words: "O Māṇava!..."
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Why is this? Subhūti!"
What is called "Tathāgata" is precisely true Suchness (*tathatā*). "Subhūti,
if anyone were to say, 'The Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' that person speaks untruth."
Subhūti! In truth, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor false within it; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
"Subhūti! As for what is called 'all dharmas,' all dharmas, they are not actually all dharmas; therefore they are called 'all dharmas.
The Commentary says:
Below this is the sixteenth section, "Seeking Instruction.
Within the twelve types of factors to be abandoned as obstacles, in order to abandon the absence of instruction, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma by which he attained anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi? and so forth.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"Subhūti, if there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me the prediction:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha,' and so forth. What is the intended meaning of this?

“If the Dharma of enlightenment could be spoken of in the same way as it was spoken by that Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I would have attained enlightenment at that time, and the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me the prophecy saying, ‘I shall attain [it]’;
because that Dharma is inexpressible, I did not attain enlightenment at that time, and for this reason, he bestowed the prophecy upon me.”
This is the meaning that should be understood.
Furthermore, for what reason are those dharmas inexpressible?
The Sūtra says: “Subhūti!...”
As for the term "Tathāgata," it refers to the true Suchness (tathatā).
Because it is pure, it is called "Tathāgata"; this designation is made because Suchness is ineffable.
Purity itself is called *tathatā* (suchness), just like genuine gold.
Or it is said:
"At the place of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, he did not attain *bodhi* with respect to the dharmas; rather, the World-Honored One attained *bodhi* by himself at a later time."
In order to eliminate this grasping, the Sūtra states:
"Subhūti, if anyone were to say that 'the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' that person speaks untruth," and so forth.
Furthermore, when the Sūtra says, "Subhūti!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata—within this, there is neither reality nor falsehood," it demonstrates that suchness is non-dual.
Why is it not unreal?
It is because of conventional expression.
As for "not false," it means that this bodhi is not non-existent in terms of worldly conventional expression.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas," what is its meaning?
It reveals that all dharmas are pure in their suchness (*dharmatā*).
"Suchness" (tathatā) means that it pervades all phenomena; this is its meaning.
Furthermore, because the intrinsic nature of all those phenomena is not established, in order to establish the ultimate truth (paramārtha), the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
"Regarding what is called 'all dharmas,' all dharmas are precisely not all dharmas; they are merely designated as 'all dharmas.
Thus it is said in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*, Volume Lower.

“World-Honored One!

The Buddha said:

If they were to say this:”

The Buddha said:

Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One.”

Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without a sentient being, without a person, and without a life-principle.
The Commentary says:
From here below, the seventeenth section is for the purpose of entering the path of realization. The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was wondrously vast," and so forth; this demonstrates that upon entering the path of realization, one attains wisdom and thereby abandons pride.
How is wisdom attained?
It is through two kinds of wisdom:
first, the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage; second, the wisdom of equality.
Once this wisdom has been attained, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and becomes certain to succeed the lineage of the Buddhas; this is the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage.
Having attained this, one is able to obtain a sublime body.
Among these, the "wondrous body" refers to the attainment of the perfection of the body, because the body has achieved ultimate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The "great body" refers to the fact that it encompasses the bodies of all sentient beings.
If one has long cherished the aspiration to be born into this family and, having been born there, attains that very body, this is called the "knowledge of equality regarding the sublime body.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of causes and conditions for equality:

first, equality in coarseness and wickedness; second, equality in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); third, equality in the application of abandonment; fourth, equality in the application of a mind free from expectations; and fifth, equality in the path realized by all bodhisattvas.
Because one attains these, one attains a "great body," for it is the great body that encompasses all sentient beings.
Within that body, because neither self nor other is established, the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One!"

Regarding the passage, "The Tathāgata speaks of the human body as wondrously great; yet it is not a great body, and for this reason the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'great body,'" the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is established within such [notions of] the wondrous body and so forth.
Such as these are what constitute the attainment of wisdom.
How does one become free from pride?
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!"
The Bodhisattva is also like this. If he were to say:
"I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," and so forth.
How can this be known? If one thinks:
"I liberate sentient beings; I am a bodhisattva."
It should be understood that such a person is one who possesses pride and is not a bodhisattva in the true sense.

To demonstrate this, the Sūtra states: "Therefore, the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are devoid of sentient beings," and so forth; for if a bodhisattva harbors the notion of a sentient being, they will not attain the sublime body or the great body.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva should speak thus:”
"One who says, 'I adorn the Buddha-lands,' is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this? "
When the Tathāgata speaks of "adorned Buddha-lands," Subhūti, what he calls "adorned Buddha-lands" is not actually adorned; it is merely designated as "adorned Buddha-lands. Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva penetrates the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, the Tathāgata calls them a true bodhisattva, a bodhisattva.
The Commentary says:
From here below begins the eighteenth [section], the upward-seeking of the stage of Buddhahood.
It should be understood that on that stage, there is further a sixfold perfection that encompasses the perfection of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*):

first, the perfection of the purity of the realm; second, the perfection of the purity of unsurpassed vision and knowledge; third, the perfection of mastery over merit; fourth, the perfection of the body; fifth, the perfection of speech; and sixth, the perfection of the mind.
For the sake of the perfection of the samāpatti of the purity of the buddha-field, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say:
'I adorn the buddha-fields.'"
"One who is thus [described] is not called a bodhisattva," and so forth.

This meaning is established for the sake of turning [the mind] toward correct practice within the common view, and for the sake of severing that [view]; therefore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established, as the Sūtra says: "That which is not an adornment is called the adornment of the land," and so on.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva penetrates the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. This statement refers to two kinds of selflessness, namely, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, when the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata speaks of 'Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva,'" it is because of the two kinds of perfect awakening regarding those two kinds of selflessness.
How are these demonstrated?
If one says, "I have accomplished this," that is the grasping at a self of persons;
"adorned lands" refers to the grasping at a self of phenomena.
This is not a bodhisattva.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."

Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? Subhūti replied:

“The Tathāgata says they are sand.

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River.

Subhūti said: “That world-system is very numerous,
World-Honored One!”

Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all dwellings of the mind are, in fact, non-dwellings of the mind; it is for this reason they are called "dwellings of the mind. Why is this?
“Subhūti! The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
The Commentary says:
Below this, the second section is for the sake of the perfection of the purity of vision and knowledge that is unsurpassed; thus the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? and so forth.
Within this, there are two kinds:
first, purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*), and second, purity of knowledge (*jñāna-viśuddhi*).

The Tathāgata does not possess only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); rather, in order to demonstrate the excellence of the purity of both knowledge and vision, he reveals that there are five kinds of eyes. Were it otherwise, one would seek only the purity of vision through the wisdom-eye.
Within this, there are briefly four kinds of eyes:

namely, those comprised of form, those comprised of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), those comprised of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and those comprised of all aspects of all that is to be known.
The inclusion of form (*rūpa*) further consists of two types: the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*). These constitute the coarse objects of the five eyes.

Because this is the power of wisdom regarding the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) within the initial inclusion of form, mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) proceeds without inversion; therefore, the inclusion of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) comes first.
Among these, the wisdom that teaches the Dharma to others—whereby a particular teaching is established for a particular person—is called the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
The effortless wisdom regarding all aspects of everything that should be known is called the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
These are called the purity of view.
As the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Like all the sands in the Ganges River"—such passages as these constitute the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*).
Within this context, "the mind abiding" refers to the minds of the three periods of time.
Regarding "of various kinds," one should know there are two types: namely, defiled and pure; that is to say, the mind associated with desire and the mind free from desire, and so forth.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the temporal divisions such as the past and so forth.

Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established within these two, the Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata says that all dwellings of the mind are non-dwellings of the mind," up to "the past mind is unattainable," and so on.
Within this, the past mind cannot be apprehended because it has already ceased;
the future mind cannot be apprehended because it does not yet exist;
and the present mind cannot be apprehended because it is, in the ultimate sense, ungraspable.
The establishment of "view" (*darśana*) is for the sake of realizing that which is to be known;
the establishment of "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is for the sake of teaching various sentient beings how to pacify their minds.
Within this purity of knowledge, it is said that the abiding of the mind is itself the non-abiding of the mind.
In this way, within the purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*), why is it not stated that "the eye itself is not [existent]"?
Because they share a single locus, and because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established subsequent to the purities of vision and knowledge, the former is also thereby accomplished.
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
If someone were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family obtain much merit by reason of this?
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"By these causes and conditions, this person shall obtain exceedingly great merit.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Subhūti! By this cause and condition, those sons and daughters of good family will acquire a vast accumulation of merit. Subhūti!

"What do you think?

"The Tathāgata speaks of the perfection of all marks, yet this is not a perfection; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'perfection of all marks.
