Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this?
If anyone says, "The Tathāgata has preached a Dharma," they slander the Buddha, for they fail to understand what I have taught.
Why is this? Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks the Dharma, that which is called "speaking the Dharma" is actually no dharma that can be spoken; it is merely named "speaking the Dharma."
The Commentary says:
Below this, the fifth [section] is for the sake of the perfection of speech; thus the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Do you think that the Tathāgata has the thought, 'I shall preach some Dharma'? and so forth.
Within this context, because he establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma; as for 'preaching the Dharma,' [it is thus]... and so on.
The Sūtra says:
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti!
"Sentient beings, sentient beings—what the Tathāgata calls 'sentient beings' are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as 'sentient beings.
The Commentary says:
From here below is the sixth [section], the Fulfillment of the Mind.
Within the perfection of the mind, there are further six aspects:

first, the foundations of mindfulness; second, the right awakenings; third, the establishment of the dharma of great benefit; fourth, the appropriation of the dharmakāya; fifth, non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; and sixth, the purity of conduct and abiding, which should be understood.
Regarding the perfection of the mind, for the sake of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the Sūtra says:

"World-Honored One, will there be sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma taught, will give rise to faith? and so forth. This passage demonstrates that, among all sentient beings, [the Buddha] manifests as the World-Honored One’s foundation of mindfulness.
That he is not a sentient being is because of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
that he is not a non-sentient being is because of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That such a person is "the foremost among the rare" demonstrates that the teaching of the ultimate truth is both uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) and consistent (*yukta*).
This passage is as previously explained.
The Sūtra says:
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One.”
“World-Honored One!
There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal, without high or low; it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because there is no sentient being, no person, and no life-span, one attains the equality of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By practicing all wholesome dharmas, one attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
The Commentary states:
Below this, secondly, regarding the perfection of that mind, for the sake of perfect enlightenment, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Does the Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? and so forth.

Within this, the phrase "there is no dharma" is intended to demonstrate both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*), having already distanced oneself from the view of existence.
Furthermore, he reveals that there are two kinds of causal conditions for bodhi:
namely, the expression "anuttara" (unsurpassed) and the expression "samyaksambuddha" (perfectly awakened).

Among these, when the sutra says, "There is not the slightest dharma by which a Tathāgata attains anuttara," this is because of the expression "anuttara"; it reveals the self-characteristic of bodhi and the characteristic of liberation of bodhi.
Within that, there is not even so much as a speck of dust of a dharma that possesses intrinsic substance; therefore, it should be known that it is neither obtainable nor existent.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Regarding the phrase "this dharma is equal," because it is the speech of the Samyaksaṃbuddha, it reveals that the characteristic of awakening (bodhi) is the equality of persons.
Within this, "equality" means that one knows oneself to be a Buddha by virtue of the dharma of awakening.

In this context, when the Sūtra states that "there is no high or low," it demonstrates that within the ultimate sense (paramārtha), the lifespan and other attributes of all Buddhas are without distinction of high or low.

The Sūtra states, "By means of the absence of a sentient being, a person, and a life-span, one attains the equality of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This demonstrates that *bodhi* possesses the characteristic of equality with respect to the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The sūtra’s statement that "all wholesome dharmas lead to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is intended to reveal the path to bodhi.

The sūtra’s statement that "as for what are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as 'wholesome dharmas'" and so forth, is intended to establish the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! Suppose there were someone who took all the Mount Sumeru kings and such heaps of the seven treasures as exist within a trichiliocosm and used them to practice giving.”

If a person, by means of this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain it to others even as little as a four-line verse, the previously mentioned merit would not equal a hundredth part of it, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part; it would not equal a kalā, nor a saṃkhyā, nor an upaniṣad part of it—it would be beyond all calculation and analogy.
Subhūti, what do you think? Do you think that the Tathāgata has the thought, "I deliver sentient beings"?
Subhūti! Do not hold such a view. Why is that?
"In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
Subhūti, if there were any real sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, the Tathāgata would possess the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "self," he does not mean that there is a self; it is only the hair-brained, ordinary worldlings who conceive of a self.
"Subhūti! Those born as ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) are, according to the Tathāgata, said not to be born; therefore they are called 'ordinary worldlings born.
The Commentary says:

Below this, thirdly, in order to designate the Dharma of great benefit within the perfection of that mind, the Sūtra says: "All the Kings of Mountains, Sumerus, within the trichiliocosm," and so forth.

Within this context, for the purpose of establishing the instruction on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Sūtra says: "Do you think that the Tathāgata has the thought, 'I deliver sentient beings'? and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "The Tathāgata possesses the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span," what is its meaning?
The Tathāgata knows according to the nature of objects of cognition (*jñeya*); therefore, if there were sentient beings, the Tathāgata would possess the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
If there is truly no self, yet one speaks of "appropriation of a self," it is in order to eliminate this attachment that the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a 'self,' he does not thereby speak of a [real] self," and so forth.
Therefore, it is only because childish ordinary persons possess such grasping that the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, those who are born as 'hair-path ordinary persons' are called by the Tathāgata 'not born'; for this reason, they are called 'born as hair-path ordinary persons.'"
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks?
Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has said, one does not see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
"One does not see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."

If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of physical marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata; therefore, it is not by the perfection of physical marks that the Tathāgata can be seen.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me by means of sound,
Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata."
That wondrous body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
its Dharma-nature cannot be seen, and that consciousness cannot know it. “Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Can a Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the perfection of the marks? Subhūti!
"Do not harbor this thought:
'The Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the perfection of physical marks.
The Commentary says:
Below this, the fourth section concerns the perfection of that mind; for the purpose of encompassing the *dharmakāya*, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"Can one see the Tathāgata through mutual accomplishment? and so forth.
Among these, the first verse demonstrates that he is not to be seen as he might otherwise appear, because he is invisible.
Why is it "unseeable"? Because all views pertain to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This person practices "perverse tranquility"; although concentration is indeed called "tranquility," one who has attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is specifically designated as a "tranquil one."

Furthermore, dhyāna is called "contemplation" (cintā) and "cultivation" (bhāvanā). Within this, "contemplation" is subsumed under mental activity (manas), while "cultivation" is subsumed under consciousness (vijñāna).
That which is termed "tranquility" refers to sensation (vedanā) and consciousness; one should know that these are subsumed within conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Those who are unable to see are those who practice according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
The second verse demonstrates how they should not see and the reasons why they should not [see], namely the first and subsequent sections.
In this regard, the verse states that "one should see the Buddha by means of the Dharma. Here, "Dharma" refers to the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
For what reason? The verse states: "The Guide takes the Dharma as his body."
Because they take suchness as their condition, the pure bodies of all Buddhas are produced; these are invisible, for one should see only the Dharma, and thus they should not be seen.
Furthermore, by what cause and condition are they invisible?
Because that dharma has the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness), it is not known through verbal expression, but is known only through self-realization (*pratyātma-vedya*).
That which does not conform to verbal expression is not "seeing," for in reality, it cannot be known [by such means].
To demonstrate this meaning, the verse states: "The essence of the Dharma is invisible," because that consciousness cannot know it.
Within this context, it is shown that the Tathāgata should be perceived by means of the Dharmakāya, and not by means of the perfection of physical marks.

"If that is so, although the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks, one should nonetheless take the perfection of physical marks as the cause for attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
To eliminate this attachment, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, what do you think?
Can a Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the accomplishment of the marks?"
"Subhūti! Do not conceive such a thought," and so forth.

This meaning clarifies that the essence of the perfection of marks is non-existent, and that awakening (bodhi) likewise does not take the perfection of marks as its cause, because marks are the intrinsic nature of form (rūpa).
The Sūtra says:
"Subhūti! If you should have this thought:"
“Those bodhisattvas who have set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speak of the characteristic of the annihilation and cessation of all phenomena. Subhūti,
do not entertain such a thought!
"To say that 'a bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the characteristic of the annihilation of all phenomena'— why is this?
Because one who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of the annihilation of phenomena."
“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River and offer them as a gift;”

If there is a bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas, this merit surpasses the previously mentioned acquired merit. Subhūti!
"This is because bodhisattvas do not grasp at merit.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
“Does a bodhisattva not take up merit?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
The Bodhisattva receives merit but does not grasp at merit; therefore, the Bodhisattva takes up merit.
The Commentary says:
Below this is the fifth section, concerning the perfection of that mind, for the sake of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Within this, there are two aspects:
first, not dwelling in nirvana; second, not dwelling in samsara.
For the sake of not dwelling in nirvana, [the Buddha said]: "Subhūti!..."
"If you should think thus:
'A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* teaches that all dharmas have the characteristic of annihilation'—and so forth."

In this regard, when the Sūtra states, "one does not speak of the annihilation of dharmas," it means that one penetrates phenomena as they truly abide; without severing any of the reflected images of birth and death, one acts with mastery within nirvāṇa for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
In this context, in order to preclude [the view of] absolute quiescence, non-abiding nirvāṇa is revealed. [One might object:
"If one does not abide in nirvāṇa, one must undergo the suffering and affliction of saṃsāra."
To eliminate this attachment and demonstrate that one does not abide in saṃsāra, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift," and so forth.
In this context, what is the meaning of the sūtra’s statements “non-self” and “patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena”?
Because the Tathāgata has attained mastery over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), he is devoid of birth and death, as well as of phenomena and self.
Furthermore, because he does not arise through the power of karma or afflictions (*kleśa*), he is without arising; therefore, they are called "non-self" and "without arising."
How can this be demonstrated?

It is said that even by merely appropriating other merits, one does not undergo suffering within saṃsāra; how much more so for the merit produced by a bodhisattva who has attained patience regarding the selflessness and non-arising of phenomena, which far surpasses those [other merits].
The Sūtra states: “Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not grasp at merit. This demonstrates that they do not abide in saṃsāra;
for if they were to abide in saṃsāra, they would indeed receive a mass of merit.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Sūtra: "Subhūti said to the Buddha:
'World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva does not grasp at merit,'" what is the meaning of this?
Because the World-Honored One has stated elsewhere that one should receive a mass of merit, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha said: 'Subhūti!'"

Regarding the statement, "The bodhisattva receives merit but does not grasp at merit; therefore, the bodhisattva takes up merit," this demonstrates that while one should receive it through skillful means, one should not grasp at it.
"Feeling" is spoken of because of its existence;
"clinging" is because of the cultivation of that path.
As with the accumulation of merit and its fruit, one should not be attached to any of them.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! If someone were to say:”
"If the Tathāgata comes or goes, stands, sits, or lies down"—
this person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this?
"The Tathāgata has nowhere to which he goes and nowhere from which he comes; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Commentary says:
From here below, within the sixth section on the perfection of mind, this is for the purification of conduct and abiding.
Within this, there are further three kinds:

first, the conduct of deportment (walking and standing); second, the conduct of mastery in the contemplation and deconstruction of name-and-form; and third, the conduct of non-attachment, which should be understood.
Regarding the conduct of the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, the Sūtra says:
"Subhūti, if someone were to say:
'The Tathāgata either comes or goes,'" and so forth.
Among these, "walking" refers to going and coming;
"standing" refers to the remaining postures.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the atoms of a trichiliocosm, and further reduce that many worlds into incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers of atoms;”
Subhūti, what do you think? Would that multitude of atoms be considered many?
Subhūti said: “That multitude of atoms is vast,
World-Honored One!”
Why is this? If this multitude of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have spoken of it as a "multitude of atoms. Why is this?
The Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms, yet it is not a multitude of atoms; therefore, the Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a trichiliocosm is not a world; therefore, the Buddha spoke of a trichiliocosm.
Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).
What the Tathāgata calls a unified whole is not a unified whole; therefore, the Buddha speaks of a unified whole.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is ineffable; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.”
Why is this? Subhūti! If someone were to speak thus:
"The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being,
and the view of a life-span. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Is what this person says correct speech? Subhūti replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and believe in them thus; in this way, they do not dwell upon the marks of phenomena.”
Why is this? Subhūti, as for what is called "the mark of dharmas," the Tathāgata says that this mark of dharmas is not a mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as "the mark of dharmas."
The Commentary says:
The second section below is for the purpose of refuting the notion that the body of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) possesses mastery over movement and abiding; thus the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the atoms of the trichiliocosm," and so forth.
Within this context, the refutations concerning the method of subtle reduction and the method of non-perception should be understood as previously explained.
The Sūtra states: "That multitude of atoms is exceedingly vast."
"Bhagavān" is the skillful means of subtle analysis.
When the Sūtra says, "If this multitude of atoms were substantially existent, the Buddha would not have called it a 'multitude of atoms,'" and so forth, this is the skillful means of non-perception.
What is the meaning of this statement?
If the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-rāśi*) were to exist as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the World-Honored One would not have said that it is "not a collection.

As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha speaks of a collection of atoms, yet it is not a collection of atoms; therefore, the Buddha speaks of a collection of atoms. This is because the substance of such a collection is not established.
If it were otherwise, even without being stated, one would naturally know this to be a collection; for what purpose, then, would it need to be stated?

As for the sutra’s statement, “The trichiliocosm spoken of by the Tathāgata,” and so forth, this is a skillful means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-upāya*); it deconstructs the aggregate of names (*nāmakāya*), and this should be understood as previously explained.
In this context, "world" (*loka*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
Because it is designated by means of a mere collection of names, the Sūtra states: "If a world were to exist as a reality, it would be a unified whole (*piṇḍagrāha*)."
Within this context, because both the world and the realm of atoms are explained together, there are two kinds of grasping: namely, grasping as a whole and grasping by differentiation.
That which exists as the categories of sentient beings and the world of sentient beings is a "lump-grasping" (piṇḍa-graha).
That which exists as atoms (paramāṇu) is "differentiated lump-grasping," because it grasps a collection of atoms.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement, “The Tathāgata speaks of a ‘unified mass,’ yet it is not a unified mass,” this is because the Venerable Subhūti establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the World-Honored One does so in order to bring such a meaning to fulfillment.
The Sūtra states, "That which is a unified aggregate is inexpressible," and so forth. What does this demonstrate?
Because it is a worldly convention, there is that grasping as a mass;
because it pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that phenomenon is inexpressible.
That ordinary person, like a child, grasps according to verbal expression; this is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Having already explained the skillful means of non-seeing, the refutation of [wrong] meanings has not yet been stated.
Within non-seeing, when entering the corresponding samādhi, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination, namely:
As for that which is not conceptually differentiated, who is it?
What is the phenomenon? What is the means?
What is meant by "non-discrimination"?
This will be explained in detail below.
The Sūtra says: "Subhūti!..."
If someone were to say,
"The Buddha taught the view of self," and so forth— these [statements] demonstrate that which is non-conceptualized.
How is this demonstrated?
Because the Tathāgata says that what non-Buddhists call the "self" is actually the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), he establishes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*);
furthermore, because he teaches that this view of a self exists, he establishes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
If there are views of "self" and "other," these are subsumed under [false] views.

Observing in this manner, when a bodhisattva enters the samādhi of correspondence, they no longer engage in conceptual discrimination; thus, this very observation serves as the skillful means for entry.
The Sūtra states: "Subhūti!
A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This indicates a person free from conceptual discrimination.
The scriptural statement "regarding all phenomena" indicates the phenomena with respect to which one does not engage in conceptual discrimination.

The scriptural statement "one should know thus, see thus, and believe thus" indicates that, by means of higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhijñāna*), one knows, sees, and gains resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) within non-conceptualization.

In this context, when wisdom knows by relying on *śamatha* and sees by relying on *vipaśyanā*, these two rely upon *samādhi* for their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Because of mastery over *samādhi*, one resolves upon the internal image of the object; that is called "resolute conviction."
When the Sūtra says, “In this way, one does not dwell in the characteristics of dharmas,” this correctly demonstrates non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

When the Sūtra says, “As for what is called the ‘characteristics of dharmas,’ the Tathāgata has said that these are not characteristics of dharmas; they are merely named ‘characteristics of dharmas,’” this demonstrates the unique meaning and the concordant meaning within the characteristics of dharmas, as previously explained.
It should be understood that the application of the samādhi-concordant methods within all such dwelling places is likewise so.

Regarding the two types—the aspiration and the gathering of the distracted—as previously explained, there is no further distinct meaning; therefore, their specific methods will not be discussed again.
The Sūtra says:
“Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, were to hold them and give them as a gift.”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who have resolved their minds on Bodhisattvahood, and who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain to others even as little as a four-line verse from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, their merit shall surpass that of the former by immeasurable, incalculable [asamkhyeya] amounts.
How does one expound for others so that it is not called "expounding," yet is indeed called "expounding"?
"All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a visual impairment, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud; they should be viewed in this way."
The Commentary says:
Below this is the third section, concerning abiding in conduct free from defilement.
Within this, there are two types:
First is non-attachment to preaching the Dharma; second is non-attachment to saṃsāra.
Regarding non-attachment to preaching the Dharma, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti!
If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds," and so forth.
What does this demonstrate?
Because there is such great benefit, one must certainly expound [the teaching];
yet, while expounding it in this manner, one remains untainted.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "How does one expound for others so that it is not called 'expounding,' yet it is indeed called 'expounding'? what is its meaning?
It demonstrates that [the ultimate] is ineffable.
One should teach that those dharmas have an expressible essence; it should be taught in this way.
If it were otherwise, it would be a defiled teaching, because its meaning would be inverted.
Furthermore, when speaking in this manner, one does not seek faith, respect, or the like, and thus teaches the Dharma without defilement.

Because it is for the sake of the undefiled flow [of the teaching], a verse in the Sūtra says: "All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a visual impairment, a lamp, and a magical illusion," and so forth.
This verse reveals four kinds of conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*):

first, the characteristic of intrinsic nature; second, the characteristic of attachment to what is dwelt upon; third, the characteristic of conforming to faults; and fourth, the characteristic of conforming to renunciation.

Among these, as for the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), it is the common characteristic of the seeing-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*); this characteristic is like a star and should be viewed in this way. Why is this?
Because that light exists within the darkness of ignorance, whereas that light does not exist within the brightness of wisdom.
The views of a self in persons and phenomena are like cataracts; one should perceive them in this way. Why?
Because they grasp at what is without meaning.
Consciousness is like a lamp; it should be viewed in this way.
Why is this? Because it is moistened by craving and grasped by clinging as conditions, it blazes forth and becomes attached therein.
Regarding the characteristic of attachment to what is dwelled upon: because one is attached to and craves perverted objects, they should be viewed as being like an illusion. Why is this?
Because it is due to perverted views.
Among these, "conforming to the characteristics of faults" refers to conforming to [the truths] such as impermanence.
The analogy of that exposed [object] demonstrates that the essence of the characteristic does not exist, because it conforms to impermanence.
The analogy of the bubble demonstrates conformity with the essence of suffering, because feeling is like a bubble.
Whatever is felt is all suffering, due to the three types of suffering; this should be understood according to their occurrence:
because that suffering arises, it is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Because it is subject to destruction, it is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*);
because it is inseparable [from the conditioned], it is the suffering of formations (*saṃskāraduḥkha*).
Furthermore, the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*) is established within the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms because of their excellence.
Among these, that which accords with the characteristic of renunciation conforms to the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Because one attains renunciation by taking them as objects of focus, selflessness is taught as renunciation.
"Conformity" refers to past and other such formations, which are illustrated by analogies such as dreams.
Those past formations are like dreams because they are merely objects of recollection;
those of the present do not endure for long, and are therefore like lightning.
Regarding the future, those coarse and evil seeds draw the mind out as if from empty space; thus they are like clouds.
Having understood in this way how the formations of the three times arise and evolve, one penetrates non-self, which demonstrates the characteristic of conforming to renunciation.
The Sūtra says:

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sūtra, the Elder Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The treatise says, in verse:
"If one hears such a meaning as this, Yet lacks awakening regarding the Mahāyāna,
I consider them to be worse than a stone, Because they ultimately lack the cause [for liberation]."
Ordinary people, regarding this profound Dharma, are unable to awaken to it or have faith in it;
most people in the world are like this, and for this reason the Dharma falls into ruin.
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra*, Vol. Lower.
